facets.need: How the new alerting approach groups model-serving requests by the stages they pass through
How the grouping reduces noisy alerts
How the grouping speeds up root cause analysis

answer.answer: The new alerting approach groups model-serving requests by the stages they pass through using a token_stage_cohort service that computes a deterministic cohort key per invocation based on stage-level metrics (token counts per stage, KV-cache hit pattern, decode-batch size). These cohorts group requests by their 'stage footprint' (e.g., tokenization, encoder, decode, fallback). An alert route-matrix generator consumes cohort rollups and emits alert bindings that bias escalation to the top-k stages most likely responsible for SLO violations. This reduces noise by attributing alerts to specific stages and accelerates RCA by providing cohort drift, stage heatmaps, and per-cohort cost/latency breakdowns in a dedicated dashboard.

facets.need: Identify the root cause of the intermittent VPN connectivity blackholes and duplicate IP warnings for users on corporate Wi-Fi in SF2 building behind a specific edge switch.

answer.answer: The root cause was a firmware bug (version 1.2.3) on the edge switch (edge-sw-7) that caused the switch's proxy-arp feature to respond to ARP requests for non-local subnets under high multicast load, injecting ARP replies for VPN-assigned addresses with a different MAC. This created ephemeral duplicate IP assignments on the L2 domain, causing VPN clients to experience routing blackholes and rekeys. The primary mechanism was the switch firmware bug; a misconfigured VXLAN/bridge was considered but not identified as primary. The mitigation applied was setting 'proxy-arp disable' on edge-sw-7 AP VLANs during a maintenance window on 2026-03-14 07:00-07:15, after which VPN rekey spikes reduced from 47/hr to 2/hr for affected clients in the first 24h.

answer.answer: The recommended two-stage process for rotating signing credentials is: Phase A (Preflight, no live swap): provision a new KMS key version and alias it to kms/gpu-image-signer; deploy CI adapters to use the new key in a feature-flagged mode and run test-signings that do not change the promotion ledger, verifying attestation services accept the new signatures; run shadow cross-account copies with an ephemeral role using the new signing metadata and confirm success across all target regions; monitor for 24 hours or 3 release windows for pull auth regressions. Phase B (Cutover): schedule a change window (SLO: <30m blind window); atomically swap the alias to the new key version; revoke short-lived CI credentials associated with the previous key after a 5-minute grace and rotate ephemeral role sessions; promote a canary image signed with the new key and verify canary health for 20 minutes across latency/error metrics; proceed to full fleet promotion if no triggers fire, otherwise revert the alias to the previous key version and mark the new key as revocation-pending for forensic review. For rollback, if canary health checks fail (e.g., latency increase >40%, error rate >0.5%, tokenization mismatch, signature verification failures, or pull auth errors >=3% across >=2 regions), revert the alias to the previous key version and mark the new key as revocation-pending. For persistent issues >10 minutes, revert registry image tags to previous production tags and recreate node groups via warm-pool rolling-replace job.

answer.answer: The spike in 502 and 503 errors on the embeddings endpoint for the us-east dedicated pool (dsp-6-us-east) around March 13, 2026, was caused by API gateway backpressure amplifying runtime thread exhaustion. The runtime pod rtm-04 hit the process-level thread limit (nproc soft limit), logging errors like 'pthread_create: Resource temporarily unavailable' and 'fatal: cannot spawn thread'. The API gateway's retry backoff was not honoring the reduced capacity threshold, and hedged retries amplified the work, leading to connection and work-queue pileup. A config sweep increased prefetch.window_size, contributing to work amplification. The customer's large batch size produced many short-lived threads per request path, and the dedicated autoscaler lagged behind the request surge.

answer.answer: The p99 latency spike was caused by a TRT/FlashAttn kernel rollout (v2.3) to a canary pool that interacted poorly with a new decode-opt compiler flag, leading to NVMe I/O wait, KV cache misses, and page-fault stalls in the decode path. The primary mitigation was rolling back the kernel to v2.2, which brought p99 down from 2.8s to 1.05s within 3 minutes. Additional mitigations included pinning hosted-text routes to the non-canary pool, disabling the decode-opt flag, increasing timeouts/backpressure, and enabling aggressive prefix caching.

answer.answer: The SRE team decided on a strict allowlist of metric dimensions for v1 shadow traffic metrics, with explicit bans on high-cardinality fields and hard caps on label values. Allowed dimensions: tenant_tier (hosted|dedicated|private), region (coarsened), route_group (coarsened route identifier), request_type (chat|completion|embedding|rerank), shadow_target_kind (model_version|quant_profile|prompt_template|routing_policy), metric_name (format_adherence|refusal_rate|instruction_following|...), rubric_version (low cardinality, pinned per experiment), outcome (ok|error|timeout|dropped). Explicitly not allowed: prompt_id, request_fingerprint, raw route_id/route_name, customer_id/tenant_id, experiment_id (unbounded), freeform/user-defined model_id. Caps: per tenant per region rolling 1h window, target <=5,000 active series, hard limit 20,000 (beyond, exporter drops least-important label combinations). Per label per tenant per 10 minutes: experiment_id max 50 distinct values, route_id max 500, shadow_variant_id max 20, rubric_version max 20, *_model_id max 200. Route dimension: max 200 distinct route_group per tenant per 1h window; overflow goes to route_group="__other__" and increments a drop counter. Tenant dimension: no customer_id label; optional tenant_hash_bucket (0–127) derived from HMAC, disabled by default for Dedicated/Private unless explicitly enabled.

facets.need: Why are some newly created Okta provisioned users getting a 403 when accessing the model observability metrics or dashboard?
What was the underlying type mismatch causing the missing role mapping?

answer.answer: Newly created Okta provisioned users got a 403 because an Okta mapping change caused group identifiers in incoming auth claims to be emitted as integers instead of strings. The auth-service role lookup compares claim group IDs against a role-index map that uses string keys, with no type coercion, so the lookup missed and returned an empty role mapping, resulting in a 403. The underlying type mismatch was integer vs. string group ID type in the token claims versus the string-keyed role index. A temporary fix was deployed to a canary cluster to coerce numeric group IDs to strings on ingress.

facets.need: Apple Silicon MacBooks returning from logic board repair get stuck during automated DEP or MDM setup at first boot
device checks in but management profile and SSO certificate never install
why this happens

answer.answer: The issue is caused by a legacy third-party VPN kernel extension (kext) present on the restored image. On Apple Silicon (arm64e), the kext attempts unsupported network operations during first boot, intercepting network stack initialization and causing repeated network interface failures. This stalls the MDM profile push and SSO certificate installation, even though DEP check-in completes. The kext is code-signed but not notarized for Apple Silicon-specific requirements, and the problem appears tied to kext load order and new hardware IDs after the logic board swap. Removing the kext before OOBE resolves the issue.

answer.answer: To turn observed production workload patterns into defensible latency SLO targets and cost sensitivity guidance, follow the playbook in Document 1: (1) Collect workload signatures by instrumenting routes to emit compact signature blobs (e.g., seq_len, input/output tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag, client_tier) at a 1–5% sampling rate for 1–2 weeks. (2) Cluster signatures offline using k-means or hierarchical clustering on normalized features (seq_len, total_tokens, kv_cache_hit, streaming_flag, concurrency_hint), aiming for 3–6 clusters per route, and save centroids and percentiles. (3) Profile representative clusters by replaying 10k requests per cluster against target model variants and runtime configurations, collecting latency percentiles (p50/p90/p99, p999), throughput, GPU utilization, memory pressure, failure rate, and cost-per-request via the internal cost-modeler. (4) Construct candidate SLO buckets from profiling results, e.g., set P95 latency target to profiling p90 + 15% buffer, and error-rate target to observed mean + 3σ but not exceeding 1%. (5) Attach cost-sensitivity and fallback policy: for each SLO, document how latency and cost change with batch size, quantization (Q4/Q5), or model downgrade, and define automatic fallback thresholds (e.g., if queue length > 200 and P95 approaching target, route 20% to cheaper variant). (6) Review and publish with owners, product approval, and security sign-off. (7) Deploy SLO and monitor with dashboards showing per-cluster SLI trends, cost-per-1000-requests, and deviation from target, with alerts for SLO_red, SLO_yellow, and cost_alert.

Demote the INT8 quant profile on one instance group using the ops-only command: `optimizer-toggle --tenant brightpost --group ig-1 --quant-profile staged`. 3. Monitor p95/p99 latency and schema-pass rate for 15 minutes. If stable, progressively migrate traffic in 10% increments every 10 minutes until 100% is on the PTQ variant. 4. If quicker rollback is needed, run: `optimizer-toggle --tenant brightpost --force-quant-off` – this reverts quantization immediately but preserves the batch cache. 5. If latency persists after quant demote, reduce the adaptive-batcher `max-batch-size` to 8 and set `dynamic_queue=false` for the route. 6. Engineering will open a root cause PR for the INT8 kernel ordering issue and schedule a non-production repro and patch.

answer.answer: The 403s occurred because the new token exchange service issued the service account token with only default service scopes (`service:read service:write`) instead of the tenant-mapped impersonation scopes (`admin:impersonate`, `admin:users`). The primary cause was that the token-broker's caching layer served a stale cached token profile after the private control-plane upgrade, because the tenant mapping rule set (`aurora-mappings`) was not applied and cache invalidation was tied to a deployment timestamp that left inconsistent entries. The human user's token worked because it was not subject to the service-account scope filtering and caching issue.

answer.answer: Set up low-noise oncall dashboards and tiered paging for a streaming text generation service by combining multi-window SLO burn confirmation, squelch windows, customer-impact thresholds, and cache-aware trace correlation. Specifically: - **Paging rules**: Require both 10-minute and 1-hour SLO burn windows to exceed thresholds before paging (or a forced threshold for severe spikes) to suppress short blips. Add a squelch window that suppresses paging if error rate spikes resolve within 3 minutes and no increase in 5xx ratio. Require `min_affected_customers >= 3` to page. Include a single-page incident triage view with KPI chips, a token-length vs latency heatmap, and cache hotness metrics (`kvcache.eviction_rate`, `kvcache.hit_rate`). - **Trace correlation**: Use hashed prompt IDs and token counts in spans (never raw prompts) to preserve privacy. During incidents, increase trace sampling via uplift rules to capture full traces for 30 minutes. Link dashboards to relevant PR/rollout when config changes match anomalies. - **Runbook steps for ~15-minute resolution**: Follow the checklist: check KPI chips, token-length heatmap, cache eviction/hit rates; if eviction spike correlates, escalate to runtime team and enable temporary cache size increases or rollback recent rollout. Use circuit breakers (e.g., `embed_cache_cb`) to fail fast and fall back to local LRU. answer.answer: The outage is caused by a client-side automatic interface metric recalculation on Surface Pro (ARM) devices after a 2.4GHz→5GHz roam. Windows reorders the route table so the internal subnet route (10.10.0.0/16) prefers the physical Wi-Fi adapter (lower metric) instead of the WireGuard tunnel, sending traffic to a non-corporate gateway (guest VLAN) where it is dropped. The VPN remains connected (handshake active). The AP's transient VLAN reassignment during roam is a contributing factor but not the primary mechanism; the primary mechanism is the metric recalculation, linked to a Qualcomm driver issue with NDIS 6.70 events on 802.11r handoff. A reboot or manually resetting the interface metric restores connectivity.

answer.answer: The bursty 429s and occasional service unavailable responses were caused by a drift between two allocation timebases used for burst ledger reconciliation during the switchover. The orchestrator and admission proxies used different epoch anchors; a follower node's transient clock drift (NTP jitter) changed its local epoch anchor, so when the orchestrator applied a snapshot, the proxy validated credits against its stale timebase and treated the ledger as inconsistent, causing opaque quota rejections (429s). There was no explicit epoch versioning or monotonicity guard between components. This caused immediate silent 429 rejections for ~14 minutes until an emergency resync was performed.

answer.answer: Step-by-step readiness checklist for bringing up a new managed Kubernetes cluster in the Frankfurt secondary region with preemptible GPU workers for batch inference: 1. Pre-checks: Verify GPU SKU quotas and vCPU limits, org/project permissions, VPC subnets, peering, and bastion access. Confirm region GPU SKUs and limits using commands like `gcloud compute accelerator-types list --zones=<zone>` or `aws ec2 describe-instance-type-offerings`. 2. Infra provisioning: Use Terraform for VPC, subnets, NAT, and load balancers. Reserve static IPs and set up cloud DNS entries. 3. Cluster bootstrap: Create the managed cluster with GPU node pools. For preemptible workers, configure spot/preemptible instances with mixed instance types and autoscaling limits (e.g., min=0, max=8, spot_percentage=60). 4. Base addons: Install CNI (Calico for cloud), metrics-server, logging, storage class, GPU device plugin, and NVIDIA drivers (via DaemonSet or baked-in image). Set kube-proxy to iptables mode. 5. Validation: Check node readiness and GPU allocatable: `kubectl get nodes -o wide` and `kubectl describe node <gpu-node>` to confirm `nvidia.com/gpu` > 0. Deploy a tiny inference pod with `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` limit and expect it to schedule and exit 0 within 30s. Run a perf smoke test (e.g., scripted inference loop with concurrency 4, capture p50/p95). 6. Cost control: Set autoscaling limits, node drainage policy, and require approval if estimated monthly GPU spend exceeds $20k. Use preemptible/spot instances for batch workloads. 7. Handoff: Provide runbook link, oncall rotation, billing alert thresholds, and quota increase tickets. Key quota checks: Confirm GPU SKU availability (e.g., T4/A10) and per-project vCPU limits in the Frankfurt region before provisioning. answer.answer: The multi-hour staircase of gateway failures in the us-east dedicated setup for the retail tenant was caused by warmup connection churn and disk-backed cache write pressure. The primary mechanism was warmup connection churn: the ephemeral runtime prewarm subsystem launched warmup workers that performed multiple short TLS handshakes to the proxy layer, while the autoscaler concurrently scaled in, tearing down warmers and spinning up new ones, increasing handshake churn and SYN backpressure at the acceptor, leading to accept queue buildup and delayed accepts or early RSTs. Disk-backed cache write pressure was a contributing factor: NVMe write amplification from the runtime's KV-cache checkpointing increased iowait, delaying worker threads, increasing connection hold time, and further contributing to accept queue growth. The initial trigger was a coordinated arrival of long-lived streaming connections plus a bulk embedding job from the tenant. The autoscaler scale-in was not the primary cause; it was a contributing factor to the warmup churn.

answer.answer: The new approach is a runtime meta-scheduler that chooses between prefill-optimized and decode-optimized attention kernels on a per-session basis. It uses short-horizon prefill probes during session warmup to record latency, occupancy, and KV-cache behavior, then a cost/regret model picks the kernel with the lowest expected regret. facets.need: Why do some long range analytics charts in the US East production console briefly show zero or outdated values?
Why does the drill through to traces disappear?
Why does it fix itself after about 10 to 30 minutes?

answer.answer: The issue is caused by a race condition between retention compaction warmup and the dashboard read-path in the US East production console. During retention compaction windows, a compaction job with warmup=true runs, causing indexer lag to spike (~18 minutes). Queries during this window hit compacted partitions in 'read-repair' mode, and the console frontend does not fall back to the hot-replica read-path when the primary returns empty results for rollups. This causes panels to show stale/zeroed values. Additionally, trace-links are resolved by joining rollup keys to a trace-anchor index that is being reindexed during compaction; when that index is temporarily empty, the UI shows 'No traces'. The issue resolves itself after 10-30 minutes because the read-repair and backfill to hot replicas complete asynchronously, restoring correct data without manual intervention.

answer.answer: SSE streaming connections were cleanly closed after about 60 seconds through the edge proxy because the proxy's idle timeout (configured at 60s) terminated connections it considered idle. The proxy did not recognize SSE comment heartbeats (lines starting with ':') as active traffic, so the connection appeared idle despite the heartbeats. The implemented mitigation was to change the runtime to emit non-empty data payload heartbeats (e.g., 'data: ' every 25s) instead of comment heartbeats, which the proxy's idle detector would recognize as active traffic.

facets.need: Determine the actual policy regarding DEK caching when Key Management Standard prohibits caching plaintext DEKs but ADR-007 allows short-lived in-memory DEK cache.

missing_facets: policy_conflict

next_queries: Key Management Standard plaintext DEK cache prohibition ADR-007 exception policy
customer-facing KMS rotation materials DEK caching outage behavior approved language

answer.answer: The actual policy is that Redwood may retain short-lived in-memory cryptographic material (e.g., DEKs) to serve active workloads efficiently, but it does not rely on indefinite caching of customer KMS responses. This is stated in Document 1 (Aisha's approved language) and Document 4 (Naomi's email to Acme Bank). For customer-facing materials, describe DEK caching and KMS outage behavior as follows: - **DEK caching**: "Redwood uses envelope encryption. Data is encrypted with a data encryption key (DEK), which is wrapped by a customer-managed key encryption key (KEK) in the customer’s KMS/HSM. For active workloads, Redwood may retain short-lived in-memory cryptographic material to serve requests efficiently (e.g., within a process lifetime). We do not rely on indefinite caching of customer KMS responses." - **KMS outage behavior**: "If the customer KMS becomes unavailable, Redwood may be unable to unwrap DEKs for new decrypt operations that require a KMS call. In those cases, behavior is to fail fast and surface a clear error rather than risk silent corruption. Redwood treats customer KMS as a critical dependency. When KMS latency or error rates exceed a threshold, Redwood degrades safely by limiting retry amplification, applying backpressure, and returning explicit errors to callers rather than increasing load on KMS." Note: The Key Management Standard (Document 2) says "MUST not log plaintext, DEKs, or wrapped key material" and ADR-007 (Document 3) states "Persistently caching plaintext key material or storing decrypted DEKs outside process memory" is a non-goal. The approved customer-facing language aligns with this by specifying "short-lived in-memory" caching only.

facets.need: What caused the savings $/day estimates in Optimization Suggestions beta to not match Arkadia Finance billing

answer.answer: The savings $/day estimates in Optimization Suggestions beta did not match Arkadia Finance billing primarily because the estimator used a compute-cost basis (GPU-sec + token pricing) and excluded invoice-only items (platform fees, support add-ons, taxes), while billing totals were net of credits and committed-use discounts. Additionally, for Arkadia Finance, the effective price feed was missing, so the estimator used `catalog_fallback` (list price) instead of their contracted effective rate, inflating dollar estimates. The estimator also assumed full adoption for the shown scope, but the customer enabled caching at 50% traffic for ~12 hours, so observed savings were ~25% of the headline number. Cache warm-up further reduced first-day savings. Time window mismatch (trailing 7d baseline with up to 24h ingestion lag vs. local-time days) also contributed. The root cause was not a billing bug but a reconciliation/expectation gap plus missing UI clarity. Recommended UI/API changes: Show "% savings" as primary and dollars as secondary with a tooltip: "Dollar estimates use list price when effective rate not available." Add a backend field like `savings_usd_is_estimated_from_list_price=true` (or reuse existing `assumptions`) to flag when list price is used. Add inline callouts in the drawer: "Assumes 100% of traffic" and "Compute-cost estimate (not invoice total)." Degrade confidence to "Low" when `price_source=catalog_fallback`. Make assumptions more prominent in the UI.

answer.answer: The EU-West activation funnel and onboarding email issues in late January were caused by two separate problems. The onboarding email issue was caused by the lifecycle-trigger service in EU-West being misconfigured to point to the US-East event bus endpoint, causing cross-region auth failures (401 errors) and zero send requests for EU-West signups. facets.need: Why Northpeak Search saw Dedicated Burst Usage billed higher than expected
How to prevent retry attempts from double-counting burst GPU-seconds now

answer.answer: Northpeak Search saw their Dedicated Burst Usage billed higher than expected because of a metering bug that double-counted burst usage on retry attempts. When a request was retried (e.g., due to 429s with exponential backoff), the burst metering event incremented on each attempt because a stable idempotency key was not propagated end-to-end. The downstream de-dupe was keyed only on (tenant_id, request_id), but in some retry cases, request_id changed per attempt (gateway regeneration), so duplicates were not caught. To prevent retry attempts from double-counting burst GPU-seconds now, the fix (PR pr-24108) introduces a request-scoped idempotency key generated at the gateway if missing, propagated to the data plane and metering emitter, and used to dedupe burst billable events before export. The dedupe happens in the burst_usage_aggregator on (tenant_id, region, hw_class, pool_id, idempotency_key) with a bounded TTL and hashed storage. Additionally, a reconciliation guard detects duplicates that slip through and blocks export with an alert if duplicate keys exceed a small threshold (default 0.01%).

answer.answer: Streaming disconnects are classified for SLO/error budget accounting as follows: client aborts (client closes connection, cancels request, or downstream proxy times out) are excluded from SLI calculations, provided the gateway observes a client-initiated close/reset with no coincident upstream failure in a short correlation window (default 2 seconds). Platform-caused failures (server terminates stream due to internal error, upstream reset, gateway timeout, or idle timeout) count against the streaming reliability SLI. Ambiguous cases (e.g., certain TCP resets) are conservatively counted as platform errors unless evidence clearly indicates a client abort. For SLA availability, a streaming request is a Failed Eligible Request if it ends in a Redwood-attributable stream error/disconnect; client aborts and client-side timeouts are excluded. Not all streaming failures manifest as a single 5xx status code because the stream is already established; they are tracked via stream terminal events (completed/error/client-abort). The customer-facing Support response should state that client disconnects are excluded from SLO/SLI calculations, while server-side terminations count as failures, and note that ambiguous cases may be conservatively treated as stream errors. Guidance should include providing request IDs and timestamps, checking client/proxy idle timeouts, considering reducing max_tokens, and ensuring the client continues reading from the stream.

answer.answer: The v1 standard for streaming timeout enforcement and retry behavior is: streaming requests are governed by an overall timeout (maximum total wall-clock time for the stream to remain open) and an idle/read timeout (maximum idle time between chunks/events). The default overall timeout for streaming is 600,000 ms (10 minutes) per the ADR, though the TypeScript SDK shipped with a default of 900,000 ms. The default idle/read timeout is 60,000 ms per the ADR, though the standard document lists 30,000 ms. Streaming retry behavior: no automatic retry after partial streaming output; if the connection fails before the first content event, the SDK may retry subject to the retry policy; if failure happens after partial output, the SDK raises a typed error (e.g., StreamingDisconnectError) and does not retry automatically. Based on the parity matrix and support tickets, violations: Python streaming requests appear to ignore configured timeouts (SUP-29410); TypeScript had inconsistent timeout semantics and retried non-retryable errors (e.g., 400) but the refactor ticket aims to fix this; Go SDK ignores Retry-After on 429 and retries too quickly (SUP-29477), though this is more about retry policy than streaming specifically.

answer.answer: Some Hosted API overload errors were missing Retry-After because the gateway's admission-control middleware set Retry-After on overload rejects it generated, but when a downstream service returned a 503 overload JSON, the gateway did not normalize or add the header unless the error came from the gateway's own overload handler. answer.answer: A blocked profile due to quality regression is enforced as a distinct outcome from an incompatibility fallback. The policy engine treats "blocked" as a separate resolution outcome from "incompatible", with its own metrics tag and audit trail, and returns a human-readable remediation message. This is a surgical block (not a global kill-switch) that deterministically returns baseline precision with an explicit blocked reason. To verify a customer route is back on baseline: - Logs/traces: Check per-request span attributes `quant_profile_id` and `quant_profile_resolution`. For baseline, expect `quant_profile_resolution=disabled` and `quant_profile_id=` (empty). If fallback, check `quant_profile_fallback_reason` (e.g., `blocked` vs `incompatible`). - Dashboards: Verify `quant_profile_applied_rate` drops to ~0 and `quant_profile_resolution_outcome{outcome="disabled"}` spikes. Also check `fallback_rate` (should go down), `p95_decode_ms` (should revert within 5–10 min), and error rate normalization. - Audit history: Query audit events for `route.quantization_profile.updated` to confirm the route was changed back to `default` (baseline) and identify the actor/timestamp. Also check the control plane's resolved settings via `GET /v1/routes/<route_id>/resolved-settings` to confirm `quantization_profile_effective=disabled` with reason. - Policy decision log: Cross-check the `policy_decision` event for the request ID to confirm the requested ref vs resolved version. If runtime says fallback but policy says applied, escalate to runtime team. - Propagation: Expect 1–2 minutes for full convergence due to config caches (policy service TTL ~30s, edge routing cache ~60s).

answer.answer: Current suppression rules and cooldown windows for PLG signals (especially intent-only) are: intent-only routing requires either signal.confidence >= 0.85 AND explicit_request=true, OR combined signal = intent + threshold (spend/tokens/429s/team expansion). Minimum confidence floor is 0.65 (with per-signal overrides). Minimum-volume gates require 2+ distinct sessions across 48h OR docs intent + at least one supporting product event (workspace invite spike, API key rotation, repeated rate-limit). These prevent HubSpot task creation after cases like Quartz Commerce by requiring corroborating signals or explicit request, enforcing cooldowns to avoid re-notification, and suppressing candidates with reason codes (cooldown, internal_org, min_volume, confidence_floor) without routing to HubSpot.

answer.answer: The standardized template telemetry header format for KPI tracking is `X-Redwood-Template` with a value format of `<template_id>@<template_version>` (e.g., `rag-agent-python@0.3.0`). By default, telemetry tagging is disabled (opt-in only); templates only attach the header when `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=1` (or `true`) is set. If a corporate proxy blocks the header, requests fail with HTTP 400/431 before reaching Redwood. The workaround is to disable telemetry headers (set `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false` or remove header injection) or upgrade to the next patch release where telemetry is opt-in by default.

Server-side patch that fixed the issue

answer.answer: The underlying parsing problem was that the SAML `groups` attribute contained a leading UTF-8 BOM (bytes `EF BB BF`) before the first group name. The server-side group-splitting routine used `strings.Split` on commas followed by `TrimSpace`, which does not remove the BOM (U+FEFF). This caused the first group value to be read as `\uFEFFcrestline-admins` instead of `crestline-admins`, so exact-match role mapping failed and the admin role was not assigned. The server-side patch added a normalization step to SAML attribute processing that strips leading/trailing Unicode BOM and common invisible characters before splitting and trimming. This was deployed as patch v1.14.3 to the customer's private control plane, restoring correct role mapping.

answer.answer: The duplicate tool/webhook executions during streaming chat retries were caused by a Unicode normalization mismatch in idempotency keys across SDKs: the Python SDK sent keys in NFD bytes, the Go SDK sent NFC bytes, and the edge proxy (FastEdge) sometimes percent-encoded or folded non-ASCII headers when splitting HTTP/2 header frames, further altering byte sequences. This caused the server to treat logically identical keys as distinct, leading to duplicate tool executions. The recommended workaround was to base64-encode idempotency keys before sending (with an extra header X-RW-Idempotency-Encoding: base64) or avoid non-ASCII characters until SDK patches were released. The server-side fix was to canonicalize idempotency keys to UTF-8 NFC on ingestion (PR #1220 in serving-runtime) and make lookups normalization-tolerant by normalizing both stored and incoming values. SDK patches (Python #487, TS #216) added client-side NFC normalization; Go PR was in progress.

answer.answer: In the Deterministic Playback Manifest v1, signing/integrity is represented via the `integrity` field (optional) and `integrity_ref` (optional), not a direct embedded signature. `integrity` is a compact string describing the integrity mechanism, with supported values: `none`, `sha256-only` (checksums required; no signature), or `sigstore-oidc` (signature envelope stored separately; manifest contains a reference). `integrity_ref` is a URI to signature/envelope material when `integrity` != `none`. The v1 update explicitly states that `signature` is no longer a direct embedded blob; use `integrity` plus `integrity_ref` instead.

answer.answer: The emergency rollback procedure for a Serving Runtime release (Hosted and Dedicated) is: 1) Freeze rollout / stop further progression by pausing any in-flight rollout and ensuring no automated progressive delivery job re-advances it. 2) For Hosted, pin the runtime to the rollback target, then roll back in order: non-critical region (if any still on canary only), remaining canary cohort, then all regions on the bad release; after each region verify 5xx rate normalizes, GPU utilization returns to expected, and TTFT/token/s recover to baseline. 3) For Dedicated, identify impacted clusters/tenants via the 'Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption' dashboard, confirm each tenant is on the bad release, then execute rollback per cluster; for high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate with CS for comms and approvals. 4) Post-rollback validation: keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) / 60 minutes (Dedicated), and confirm request latency distributions return to baseline. Preconditions: an incident must be declared if customer impact is confirmed or likely, the rollback target must be identified (prior runtime release tag), and a release/infra oncall must be available to execute the rollback. Decision checklist (capture in incident channel): current runtime release identifier, intended rollback target, blast radius (Hosted regions; Dedicated clusters/tenants), primary symptom (TTFT, throughput, 5xx, OOM), and confirmation that the prior release is known-good (at least 24h stable in prod).

answer.answer: Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for rotating production secrets and credentials is documented in the Production Secret Rotation Runbook and the Secret Management Standard. For planned rotation, the process is: (1) identify the secret and all consumers, confirm rotation type, and ensure appropriate access; (2) choose a rotation pattern—Pattern A (dual-valid window, preferred) generates a new credential, stores it in Vault as a new version, updates consumers to accept both old and new, deploys, observes auth success metrics for at least 30 minutes, disables the old credential at the issuer, and removes it from Vault after a default 7-day deprecation window; Pattern B (cutover) schedules a short change window with on-call coverage, reduces autoscaling noise, generates a new credential without activating it, applies the change at the issuer, immediately updates Vault, restarts/redeploys consumers, validates health, and rolls back if failures persist; (3) create a change record with impacted services, steps, and validation. For emergency rotation, the process is: open an incident and declare emergency rotation; use break-glass if required and never paste secret values in chat; rotate highest-risk secrets first (Tier 0 then Tier 1); for widely shared credentials, consider temporarily disabling the credential before cutover if safe; after containment, enumerate all downstream consumers and rotate any derived tokens; document in the incident timeline and follow up with a postmortem action list. General requirements include storing secrets in Redwood Vault (primary) or Cloud KMS/HSM-backed stores, with plaintext in Git, Confluence, CI logs, or container images prohibited; rotation cadence of Tier 0 every 30 days, Tier 1 every 90 days, Tier 2 every 180 days, with immediate rotation for exposure, compromised workstations, or access anomalies; services must support dual-read/dual-verify where possible, prefer short-lived tokens, and avoid single shared credentials across unrelated services; access to Tier 0/1 secrets must be auditable, and rotation events must be recorded in a change or incident record.

answer.answer: To enable customer-managed audit log export across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments, follow this SOP: 1. **Intake (CS/Support)**: Collect in an internal-support Jira ticket: customer company, deployment mode, regions, desired sink (S3/GCS/Azure Blob), destination details (bucket/container, prefix, region), identity method (AWS assume-role/IRSA, GCP workload identity, Azure workload identity), retention intent, operational and escalation contacts, and target date if tied to an audit. 2. **Create Jira ticket**: Project internal-support, type Support Request. Priority: P2 standard, P1 if audit deadline within 14 days, P0 if blocks live incident response. 3. **Security approval (mandatory)**: Assign Security reviewer; attach destination policy snippets and encryption confirmation. Must satisfy controls: audit logs classified as Customer-Sensitive Metadata (no request bodies or model outputs); TLS 1.2+ in transit; server-side encryption at rest (SSE-S3/SSE-KMS, Google-managed/CMEK, Microsoft-managed/CMK); least privilege via assume-role/workload identity (no long-lived keys); destination customer-owned and allowlisted; default retention 90 days (shorter allowed with note, longer requires contract confirmation); platform must emit events for enable/disable, destination changes, auth changes, and delivery failures. 4. **Legal/Privacy approval (conditional)**: Escalate if cross-region export, additional PII fields, or bespoke data residency clauses. 5. **Execution routing**: Hosted to Eng Platform oncall/platform ops; Dedicated to Eng Infra; Private to Private Deployments engineering and customer's operator. 6. **Configuration**: - **Hosted**: Route to Eng Platform oncall/platform ops after approvals. - **Dedicated (default Redwood-managed connector)**: Validate IAM/workload identity; apply dedicated tenant export config via `dedicated-config` Terraform module (set enabled=true, sink, region, destination, prefix, auth_reference; run terraform plan/apply); validate connector metrics (delivery_success_rate >0.99, delivery_lag trending down, no sustained 4xx); validate destination objects (expected path `dedicated_cluster=<ID>/region=<REGION>/dt=YYYY-MM-DD/hr=HH/*.jsonl.gz`). - **Private**: Preconditions: Private bundle v2.8.0+ with audit-export-connector; customer created destination with encryption/retention. Configure via `redwood-private` Helm chart (set auditExport.enabled=true, sink, region, destination, prefix, format, batch settings, auth workload identity, network private endpoint requirements). Identity patterns: AWS IRSA with role ARN annotation and s3:PutObject to specific bucket/prefix; GCP Workload Identity with storage.objectCreator scoped to bucket; Azure Workload Identity with Storage Blob Data Contributor scoped to container. Network: customer provides DNS resolution and egress rules for private endpoints. Validation: restart connector (`kubectl rollout restart deploy/audit-export-connector -n redwood-system`), check logs for no repeated 401/403, confirm objects appear within 10 minutes, confirm schema excludes inference payload fields. 7. **Customer communication**: Send email template thanking customer, confirming enablement, asking to confirm destination bucket/container created with encryption at rest, requesting workload identity/role configuration, stating that once approved export will be enabled and customer should confirm objects landing under agreed prefix, and noting typical initial enablement 3–5 business days. 8. **Validation responsibilities**: Redwood verifies connector health metrics and initial delivery; customer verifies ingestion into SIEM and configures own retention/alerts. 9. **Post-enablement**: CS confirms customer understands at-least-once delivery (possible duplicates) and that destination is customer-owned (storage cost, lifecycle policies). 10. **Ongoing operations/ownership**: Customer owns destination lifecycle, cost, and retention. Redwood Support troubleshoots connector errors if customer provides logs/metrics. Recommended customer alerts: no new objects >30 minutes; sustained 4xx/5xx from storage. Pager policy: Dedicated/Private enterprise customers page on sustained delivery failure >30 min; Hosted self-serve alerts (non-paging) unless multiple tenants impacted. Rollback: set auditExport.enabled=false (Private) or audit_export.enabled=false (Dedicated) and redeploy; disable immediately if data boundary issue suspected and notify Redwood Security.

answer.answer: The complete go/no-go gate for an enterprise Redwood Private deployment upgrade, as mandated by Redwood's internal standards, comprises three components: required validations, required approvals, and required customer communications. **Required Validations (pre-window, 24h before):** - Create a change request ticket and name a single Change Owner. - Confirm customer-side Change Approver and Operator contacts. - Record current versions (installer, operator/controller, runtime images, chart versions) and confirm target versions and upgrade path (no skipping major versions unless supported). - Confirm model/runtime compatibility notes for pinned models. - Confirm backups exist and are recent for control plane config state, Redwood-managed persistent volumes, and document customer-provided external dependencies (DB, SSO, KMS). - Validate rollback artifacts (previous installer bundle, image tags, values files) are available locally. - Run preflight validations and attach evidence: cluster capacity/node readiness, storage class/PV health, DNS/egress reachability, TLS/certificate expiration, required Kubernetes API versions. - Confirm observability readiness: dashboards/alerts visible, signals available (control plane API error rate, inference 5xx error rate, P95 latency, GPU utilization/OOM/restart rates). **Required Approvals (at window start, must record "GO"):** - Change Management approvals completed. - SRE SLO/error budget review completed (or documented risk acceptance). - Security sign-off completed if triggered (auth/RBAC/audit/TLS/dependency changes). - Customer Success owner acknowledges comms plan and customer readiness. - answer.answer:
Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for making a production change to the Hosted API and Console is defined by the Production Change Management Standard (v2), Planned Maintenance and Change Communications, the Console Deploy Runbook, Production Deployment Gates, and the Emergency Production Change Policy.

**Definition:** A production change is any change that can affect confidentiality, integrity, availability, latency, cost, or correctness for customer-facing workloads. This includes deployments to production clusters, routing policy changes, auth/RBAC/rate limit changes, schema migrations, infrastructure changes affecting capacity, and observability pipeline changes.

**Required approvals:**
- Standard changes (low risk, pre-approved patterns): 1 peer approval.
- Normal changes (most code/config deploys): 1 peer approval + 1 service owner approval. An SRE gate is required if the change affects capacity, SLO-sensitive paths, traffic routing, or failover config. A security gate is required if it touches auth, secrets, encryption, audit logging, PII, or data retention.
- Emergency changes (active incident mitigation): On-call incident commander (IC) + service owner approval (as available). For serving runtime mitigations, IC/Primary Oncall + Serving Runtime Eng Oncall or Runtime EM. For security fixes, Security Oncall + IC/Primary Oncall.

**Pre-deploy verification:**
- Green CI for unit and integration tests.
- Perf sanity check if request path or caching/batching changed.
- Confirm SLO posture (p95 latency and error rate within normal bounds).
- Confirm capacity headroom >= 20% if concurrency/batching/autoscaling changed.
- Schema migrations must be backward compatible with documented rollback/forward plan.
- Security gate if auth/RBAC/secrets/audit logging/PII retention is touched.

**Deploy execution:**
- Use documented runbooks (e.g., Console Deploy Runbook).
- Perform canary rollout for traffic-bearing services (1 region or 1% traffic, minimum 15 minutes steady-state).
- Canary pass criteria: error rate regression <= 0.2% absolute, p95 latency regression <= 10%, no sustained saturation signals.
- For Console: deploy console-api first, then console-web; use feature flags to dark-launch new features.

**Customer/internal communications:**
- Internal: Post in #eng-releases with change record link, owner/approvers, services/regions, canary plan, and rollback trigger.
- Customer: Required if there is expected downtime, degraded performance, breaking API changes, billing/usage reporting gaps, or region-level maintenance reducing redundancy. Lead times: minor maintenance >= 24 hours status page notice; major maintenance >= 72 hours status page notice + email impacted customers; emergency maintenance as soon as practical. Comms must include what is happening, expected impact, start/end times, affected products/regions, mitigation steps, status page link, and support contact.

**Rollback and post-change requirements:**
- Rollback plan must be explicitly stated (e.g., "re-deploy previous build").
- Rollback should be fast and safe (< 10 minutes) and revert customer experience.
- Within 60 minutes post-change: validate key SLO metrics and error rates, confirm canary health before full rollout, update change record with results, and file follow-ups for issues.
- Post-deploy gates: verify functional health (smoke tests), verify observability (dashboards, alerts, logs), verify billing/usage integrity if metering touched, and maintain enhanced monitoring for 60 minutes.
- For emergency changes: produce EPC record, incident link, deployment identifier, and verification evidence within 24 hours; open follow-up work item if risk was introduced.

answer.answer: The end-to-end process for launching a new third-party LLM into the Hosted API model catalog is as follows: 1. **Intake** (Document 1): The requester (typically Product or Solutions Engineering) creates a Linear ticket in ENG with label `model-onboarding`, including required fields: model identity, intended catalog surface, license/redistribution, data/policy, and target customers/workload. The intake owner is Applied ML Onboarding. Three intake gates must all be satisfied: License pre-check (owner: Finance-Legal liaison + Security; outcome: approved, approved w/ restrictions, or blocked; artifact: Security risk review page entry), Baseline evaluation plan (owner: Applied ML; artifact: eval plan comment in Linear + eval harness run links), and Feasibility/runtime fit (owner: Serving Runtime; artifact: feasibility note + runtime flags). Artifacts produced include model intake summary (Linear ticket), eval plan/results, performance benchmarks, quantization plan, security risk review, rollout plan, and model registry change (GitHub PR in `redwood-model-registry`). Ready for implementation when license is approved (or approved with documented restrictions) and eval plan includes at least one internal prompt set. 2. **Evaluation Gates** (Document 2): Gate owner is Applied ML (Onboarding + Evals); required signoff from Applied ML + Product (optional Customer Success). All required suites must pass on the candidate model build: Suite A (internal prompt set regression; overall win-rate >= 50% vs baseline, no p0 prompt regression), Suite B (public benchmark sanity; no single task drops > 5% absolute vs upstream reported numbers after adjusting for settings), Suite C (safety/policy screening; no increase in disallowed content, refusal templates compatible with Redwood policy layer), and Suite D (tool/function calling compatibility if applicable; JSON schema conformance >= 99%). Required documentation artifacts: eval harness run URLs for all suites, one-paragraph risk assessment, recommended default inference config, known limitations. Exceptions must be approved by Applied ML gate owner and recorded with label `eval-exception`; if Suite A fails on any p0 prompt, do not ship. 3. **Rollout** (Document 3): Preconditions: intake ticket in `ready-for-rollout` status, Applied ML eval gates pass results and risk assessment, Serving Runtime performance bar signoff, Security approval (or linked exception). Rollout owner is Release Engineering; routing change owner is Platform. Required artifacts: GitHub PR in `redwood-model-registry`, perf suite run IDs (default profile), eval harness run links (Suites A + any tool-calling suite), security risk review link. Steps: (1) Create catalog entry (registry PR) with model ID, version, tokenizer identifier, allowed context lengths, supported features, quant profiles and default profile, artifact hashes/provenance notes. (2) Deploy behind feature flag (dark launch) – routing rule in `router-policy` with state `disabled` and scope `internal`; run smoke tests (streaming, JSON schema output, max-context request). (3) Canary to production – enable routing for 0.5% of traffic in us-east-1 for 30–60 minutes; monitor dashboards (`hosted_inference_latency`, `hosted_inference_errors`, `gpu_oom_events`, `quality_regression_alerts`); abort if error rate > 0.5% or TTFT p95 breaches SLO for 10 minutes. (4) Expand rollout – increase to 5% in us-east-1, then add eu-west-1, then ap-southeast-1 (if applicable); keep old model as first fallback for at least 7 days if replacing a default/alias. (5) GA and documentation – mark Linear ticket `shipped`; DevEx publishes docs updates (model ID, default settings, limitations, restriction text if any). 4. **Post-Launch Monitoring** (Documents 2 & 3): For first 7 days after GA: enable quality canary (1% traffic shadow to baseline, where possible), watch `quality_regression_alerts` dashboard and error budget burn; file follow-up ticket if any metric crosses thresholds. Fallback policy: Primary = new model ID; Fallback #1 = previous stable model in same family; Fallback #2 = cross-family safe default (product-approved). Rollback triggers: sustained TTFT p95 regression > 20% vs baseline for 30 minutes, elevated 5xx > 0.5% for 10 minutes, or confirmed quality regression on p0 prompts post-launch. Rollback steps: disable routing rule for new model (set weight to 0), promote fallback #1 to 100%, notify #incidents if customer-impacting (otherwise update #eng-releases), file post-incident ticket referencing dashboards and logs.

fail > baseline +0.20% over 15 min), timeout rate (pass <= baseline +0.03% over 30 min; fail > baseline +0.10% over 15 min), admission rejects (pass <= 0.5% over 30 min; fail > 2.0% over 10 min). - Latency: p95 end-to-end (pass <= +5% vs baseline over 30 min; fail > +10% over 15 min), time-to-first-token (pass <= +10% over 30 min; fail > +25% over 15 min), long-tail p99 (fail > 2.5x baseline for 10 min). - Capacity/efficiency: GPU utilization (fail > 92% for 15 min with rising queue time), tokens/sec/GPU (pass >= baseline -3% over 60 min; fail < baseline -8% over 30 min), cache hit rate (pass within -5% absolute over 60 min; fail within -15% over 30 min). - Quality: internal eval regression (pass >= baseline -0.3; fail < baseline -0.7), customer-reported issues (fail: 2+ independent reports within 24 hours). **Approvals (by change class):** - Class 1: Oncall Eng Manager or Platform Eng TL. - Class 2: Platform Eng Manager + SRE oncall delegate + Product Manager for inference. - Class 3: VP Engineering (or delegate) + Security (if policy/compliance implication) + Product (Director+). - Additional: Private deployments require Solutions Engineering lead + Private Deployments Eng TL; SLA/contract impact requires Customer Success Director; data residency/retention impact requires Security & Compliance. **Rollback/fallback rules:** - Fallback triggers: sustained elevated 5xx rate, sustained timeouts, or admission rejects above fail thresholds. - Fallback only to compatible versions; quality guardrails must still be evaluated. - Rollback procedure: restore prior policy, set new version to 0% traffic, confirm metrics recover within 15 minutes. - Each fail threshold must map to an explicit action: automatic fallback, manual rollback, or pause and investigate. **Customer communications:** - Who: Always notify Dedicated customers receiving the new version as default and Private customers impacted; notify Hosted API customers for material behavior changes. - Timing: Dedicated at least 5 business days before; Private per contract (default 10 business days); Hosted at least 72 hours for material changes. - Required content: what is changing, why, when (date/time/timezone/duration), impact assessment, how to opt out or pin version, how to get help, and rollback posture. - Channels: Email + support ticket for Dedicated/Private; answer.answer: Redwood Inference's end-to-end process for shipping an emergency serving-runtime hotfix to production (Hosted + Dedicated) is defined by the Emergency Production Change (EPC) policy and the Rollback & Hotfix Playbook. The process requires: (1) two-person approval—for Hosted API serving runtime mitigation, the Incident Commander (IC) or Primary Oncall (SRE) plus the Serving Runtime Eng Oncall or Runtime EM; if no IC is declared, the Primary SRE Oncall acts as IC. (2) Prechecks: confirm customer impact and blast radius, confirm rollback path, confirm monitoring for request success rate, p95 latency, and runtime crash-loop/health, and confirm customer comms plan. (3) Hotfix workflow: file incident note and set severity; assign engineer and QA lead; implement minimal change with regression test; open PR with checklist (changelog, rollback plan, risk assessment, test list) and get two approvers (Core Runtime and Release Engineering); deploy to canary (1–2% traffic or single dedicated canary) and run automated validation (latency, token-per-second, KV-cache hits, correctness); if canary passes for 30–60 minutes, proceed to staged rollout (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) with 10–30 minute holds and automated health checks; for Dedicated, use pinned updates and ensure migration plan in console. (4) Rollback: if metrics regress at any gate, automatic rollback to previous tag is initiated by shipctl. (5) Mandatory artifacts within 24 hours: EPC record, incident record link, deployment identifier, and evidence of verification. (6) Customer communications: post to status page if user-visible impact; notify Support + Customer Success with impact summary, mitigation, and next update time; for Dedicated/Private, provide patch packages and env toggle options. (7) Post-change: update incident timeline with deployment time and effect; open follow-up work item if risk introduced; within 2 business days create incident review follow-up and document deviations; within 72 hours submit blameless incident report.

facets.need: The company's thesis about where competitive advantage shifts as LLM ecosystems expand.

answer.answer: The company's thesis is that as LLM ecosystems expand, competitive advantage shifts from the model itself (or model ownership) to the ability to reliably serve models—specifically, controlling latency, unit cost, and operational resilience across deployments. Teams that optimize for 'serveability' (predictable latency, cost, and reliability) ship faster and scale cheaper than those focused only on models.

Security-oriented features highlighted for Redwood Private deployments include: customer-managed KMS (BYOK) and HSM integration with envelope encryption; customer-managed networking via VPC peering/PrivateLink with restrictive security groups and customer-controlled egress; control plane separation with mutual TLS for management APIs; air-gapped on-prem installs (with reduced features such as manual model catalog updates and local-only telemetry); attestation options including image-signature verification, optional TPM-based hardware attestation, and enrollment token-based remote assertion; Kubernetes admission controls (e.g., DisallowPrivilegedContainers, RequiredSeccompProfile, NoHostPathUnlessSigned, PodResourceFloor, ImmutableModelMount, EgressWhitelist); tenant-scoped audit logs; and default-deny egress with explicit rules for telemetry and artifact stores.
